title: 1MW No. 322: That's Not What I Meant
author: McKeown, Greg
summary: Greg McKeown argues that the costliest failure in leadership communication isn't misunderstanding itself but confident misunderstanding — conviction built on an error that then gets amplified by exactly the competence and follow-through that make a leader effective. He introduces his 'Signalist Circle' framework, built from two paired 'wisdom pairs': Listen/Speak (making it safe for another's signal to emerge, then having the courage to voice your own) and Reflect/Confirm (using your own words to unlock someone's intended meaning, then letting them use theirs to verify yours). The piece frames this as intentionally simple rather than simplistic, positioning it as the discipline of testing understanding rather than assuming it. It closes with a concrete four-step script — listen, restate their meaning in your own words, ask what you got wrong, then make your own point — meant to convert the framework into an immediate conversational habit.
points: Names 'confident misunderstanding,' not plain misunderstanding, as the costliest failure — because conviction mobilizes talent and strategy behind the wrong reality.

Splits communication into two paired disciplines: Listen/Speak (make space for their signal, then risk voicing yours) and Reflect/Confirm (use your words to unlock their meaning, let them verify yours).
Gives a literal four-step script: listen, restate their meaning, ask 'what did I get wrong,' then make your own point only after theirs.
Frames the goal as accuracy sufficient to act on shared reality, not merely as being a generically 'good listener.'
quotes: The greatest bottleneck to understanding is not misunderstanding. It is confident misunderstanding.

Nothing is more costly than confident misunderstanding, especially when we know how to turn conviction into action. When that conviction rests on an error, our strengths begin working on its behalf: talent solves the wrong problem, strategy organizes around the wrong reality, and execution accelerates in the wrong direction.

Every consequential conversation carries two signals: what they are trying to convey and what you are trying to convey. If either one is lost, whatever happens next is built on only part of the available reality.
Listen and Speak belong together. Listening means making it safe for their signal to emerge. Speaking means having the courage to let your signal emerge.
Reflect and Confirm belong together, too. Reflecting means using your words to unlock their intended meaning. Confirming allows them to use their words to translate yours.
This is simple, but it is not simplistic. It is simplicity on the other side of complexity.
The point of the Signalist Circle is not merely to be understanding. It is to understand accurately enough to act on the same reality.
